title: The Northgate Library Relocation and the Peer-Review Workshop
instructions: 本材料为模拟学术英语练习，不是官方雅思考试，也不代表任何分数等级。听力有四个部分，共40题（第1-10题基于Section 1，第11-20题基于Section 2，第21-30题基于Section 3，第31-40题基于Section 4）。请先听录音（或阅读录音文本），然后回答问题。所有答案必须来自录音原文。填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过字数限制。选择题请选择最佳选项。判断题请选择 True、False 或 Not Given；选 Not Given 时，说明原文缺少哪个必要事实。
transcript:
Section 1: Social Dialogue

Woman: Hello, is this the temporary library help point?
Man: It is. I'm Owen, one of the library assistants. How can I help?
Woman: I'm Priya. I'm a second-year student in the biology department. I've just moved into the halls of residence, and I'm completely lost.
Man: Don't worry, you're not the first. The Hartley Building is closed, so everything has been moved to the old sports hall.
Woman: Right. So where exactly is that?
Man: It's on the north edge of the campus, next to the boathouse. If you come out of the main teaching building, turn left at the fountain, and follow the path past the car park. It takes about twelve minutes on foot.
Woman: Twelve minutes. That's not too bad. And can I still borrow books?
Man: Yes, you can. But most of the collection is in storage, so you request items online and collect them here the next working day. The request service is free.
Woman: Good. What about the opening hours?
Man: We open at eight in the morning on weekdays and close at eleven at night. At weekends we open at nine and close at eight.
Woman: That's later than I expected.
Man: Yes, the college extended the hours because of the complaints. There's also a minibus after nine in the evening, every half hour, back to the halls.
Woman: Perfect. Is there anywhere quiet to study?
Man: There's a silent zone at the eastern end of the hall, and a separate quiet reading room with forty seats. But the silent zone fills up quickly, so come before ten if you want a place.
Woman: Understood. Is there a café?
Man: There is, run by the students' union. It's small, and it closes at six. There's also a vending machine near the entrance.
Woman: One more thing. I have a presentation next week, and I need a quiet room to rehearse. Can I book one?
Man: Not in the temporary building, I'm afraid. The group study rooms are all in the Hartley Building, and they won't reopen until August. But you can book a small seminar room in the teaching building through the student portal.
Woman: I'll do that. Thanks, Owen.
Man: You're welcome. And good luck with the presentation.

Section 2: Social Monologue

Good morning, everyone. This is a recorded message from the Northgate College volunteering office about the autumn bird survey. The survey is part of a national citizen science project, and we need volunteers from across the college.

The survey runs for three weekends, starting on Saturday the fourth of October and finishing on Sunday the nineteenth. Volunteers are asked to choose a short route of about one kilometre, either on campus or in the streets near their accommodation, and to walk it slowly once a week, early in the morning, starting at seven o'clock. Each walk takes about ten minutes, but please allow half an hour in total for recording your results.

You do not need to be an expert. We will provide a simple identification guide and a free one-hour training session, which will be held in the teaching building on the evening of Wednesday the first of October, from six until seven. Please bring a phone if you have one, because the records are submitted through a mobile application. If you do not have a smartphone, paper forms are available at the help point.

There is one important rule. Please record only the species you are confident about. If you are unsure, mark the sighting as uncertain, and an expert will check it later. This may feel like you are providing less information, but it makes the data much more reliable.

At the end of the survey, all volunteers will receive a summary map showing the birds recorded in their area, and the three volunteers who record the most species will receive a small book about urban wildlife. To join, sign up at the volunteering office by Friday the twenty-sixth of September, or send an email to the address on the college website. Thank you, and we hope to see you at the training session.

Section 3: Academic Discussion

Tutor: Come in, both of you. Sit down. So, this is your mid-project review. Daniel, let's start with you. Remind me what you're working on.
Daniel: I'm looking at how students prepare for oral presentations, and whether rehearsal actually improves their performance.
Tutor: Right. And Mei, your project?
Mei: Mine is about the bird survey. I'm investigating whether volunteers record more species as they become more experienced.
Tutor: Good. Those are quite different, but both involve observation. Daniel, what have you found so far?
Daniel: I've interviewed four tutors, and I've recorded three student presentations. The tutors all said that delivery matters more than accent, which surprised me.
Tutor: That's consistent with what I've read. But four tutors is a small sample. You should be careful about generalising.
Daniel: Yes, I know. I'm hoping to interview two more before the end of the month.
Tutor: Good. And Mei, how is the data collection going?
Mei: It's going well, but I've hit a problem. Some volunteers are much more skilled than others, so the number of birds they record goes up over time. I'm not sure whether that's a real change in the birds or just a change in the observers.
Tutor: That's a well-known issue. It's usually called observer effort. Have you thought about how to deal with it?
Mei: I was thinking of comparing each volunteer's first walk with their last walk, rather than comparing volunteers with each other.
Tutor: That's a sensible approach. It controls for differences between people. Daniel, does your project have a similar problem?
Daniel: A bit. The students who volunteered to be recorded might be more confident than the ones who didn't.
Tutor: Exactly. That's a self-selection problem. You should mention it in your limitations section. Now, let's talk about the write-up. The draft is due on the fourteenth of November, and the final version on the twelfth of December. Mei, have you started writing?
Mei: I've written the methods section, but not the discussion.
Tutor: Start with the limitations, then. It's often easier to write when you know what you can't claim. And Daniel, don't leave the conclusion until the last minute. One more thing: both of you need to submit an ethics form before you do any more interviews or observations. The deadline for that is the thirtieth of September.
Daniel: We've already submitted ours.
Tutor: Good. Then I'll see you both in two weeks.

Section 4: Academic Lecture

Good afternoon. Today I want to explain how a peer-review workshop is organised in our department, and why we run it the way we do. This is a practical lecture, so I'll describe the stages in order.

First, a word about purpose. A peer-review workshop is a meeting in which students read and comment on each other's drafts before those drafts are submitted for assessment. It is not a marking session, and students are not asked to give grades. The aim is to help the writer see what a reader actually understands, which is often different from what the writer intended.

Second, the preparation stage. About ten days before the workshop, each student uploads a draft of no more than two thousand words to the shared folder. Everyone is then assigned two drafts to read, and these assignments are made by the tutor, not chosen by the students, so that friends do not automatically review each other. Readers are given a short form with three questions: what is the main argument, which section is least clear, and what evidence is missing. The form is deliberately simple, because open-ended comments tend to be vague.

Third, the workshop itself. We meet for ninety minutes. In the first twenty minutes, each writer describes their draft in two minutes and then listens without speaking while the two readers give their comments. The writer may take notes but may not argue. This rule, which some students find frustrating at first, is designed to make the writer listen rather than defend. In the remaining time, the group discusses two or three common problems that appeared in several drafts.

Fourth, the follow-up. Within three days of the workshop, each writer produces a short revision plan of about two hundred words, listing the changes they intend to make and the reasons for them. The plan is submitted to the tutor, who comments on it briefly. The revised draft is then submitted for assessment two weeks later. Students are not required to accept the readers' suggestions, but they are required to explain why they accepted or rejected them.

Why do we insist on this process? There are three reasons. Firstly, readers notice problems that writers cannot see in their own work, particularly problems of structure. Secondly, the discipline of commenting on someone else's writing improves the commenter's own writing, because it makes them more aware of how texts are organised. Thirdly, the revision plan creates a record of thinking, which is useful when a student later asks for feedback or appeals a mark.

There are, of course, limitations. Students sometimes give comments that are too general, such as 'it's good' or 'it needs more detail'. We try to reduce this by giving examples of useful comments in the first session. Some students also feel that the process takes too much time, and it is true that it adds about four hours of work per draft. However, the department's own review of results found that students who attended at least two workshops in a term improved their marks by an average of six per cent, compared with those who attended none. That figure should be treated with caution, because attendance is voluntary and motivated students may simply work harder anyway.

In conclusion, the workshop is designed to make writing visible: it turns a private activity into a structured conversation. Next week, we will look at how to write the revision plan itself, and I will show you two examples, one strong and one weak. Please bring your drafts to that session.

grammar.title: 被动语态、顺序连接词、定语从句与分词短语
grammar.explanation: 被动语态表示主语是动作的承受者，结构为be+过去分词。顺序连接词如first, second, then, finally用于组织步骤。定语从句用who, which, that等引导，修饰前面的名词。分词短语用现在分词或过去分词作定语或状语，使句子更简洁。
grammar.example: The decision, which was taken by the college's estates committee in March, follows an engineering report.

answers: Firstly, the draft is uploaded. Secondly, two readers are assigned.

questions.evidence: Firstly, readers notice problems that writers cannot see in their own work.
